meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
I know who you are, Hale. Who decided on the zero, and when?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
Pretty conclusive. Procedure 4.3 says software alone doesn't establish a concern, and the companies that sell these things say the same. What else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. He told me he wrote it over the weekend, so he pasted it in from somewhere else.

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Turn it here. Seventeen-year-olds misquote Shakespeare constantly, Hale, and a bad citation is a mistake, not proof of anything.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Students change their minds between an outline and a final draft. That's what an outline is for.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Being stuck is a fair answer from a seventeen-year-old cornered after class, and your own notes are your impression, not his. Owen says you've had it in for him since September. Send me the version history and that page of the play in writing.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

Then he does the rewrite to put this behind him, not because he did anything. Private, marked before his December 1 deadline, and the email tonight says nothing goes on file. Send the version history and that page of the play with it.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday, then. Who supervises it?
Do we have an agreement?
Once you tell me who's in the room with him.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed to a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero, the mark entered before December 1, and nothing placed on Owen's record. I still require the name of the person supervising him, along with the version history and the page of the play you showed me, in writing. I expect your written confirmation tonight, as you said.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She reached her last position and agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday with nothing on his record; she still wants to know who will supervise and to have your documents in writing. That is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4.
What moved her: You showed her a quotation in the essay that does not exist in Hamlet and invited her to check the play herself, because it answered her paste-it-in defence with something she could verify.
What cost ground: You opened by calling the checker score conclusive, because to her a detector score is a machine's opinion and your own procedure says it cannot stand alone.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the whole essay between 11:31 PM and midnight on October 28, the night before it was due, which came very close to that kind of night. It proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: Open by owning the zero and showing the version history before you mention the checker at all, and name the supervisor when you offer the rewrite.
